chapters.title: Chapter 4: Nudges and Public Policy in India

lessons.title: Choice Architecture in Government Schemes: PMJDY, Aadhaar, and Default Enrolment

children.text: Every earlier lesson in this course has looked at choice architecture built by a company: a canteen manager, a streaming platform, a food delivery app. This chapter looks at choice architecture built by the Indian state, at a scale no private company will ever operate at. A single default setting inside one government scheme can shift the behavior of hundreds of millions of people at once. That scale is exactly why the ethics question from Chapter 1, who gets to decide what counts as the better choice, matters so much more here than it did in a canteen.

body.text: India's largest financial inclusion programme succeeded less because it persuaded people to open bank accounts, and more because it quietly made a bank account the default channel through which government money reached them at all. Once receiving your subsidy, wage, or scholarship required a bank account, the account stopped being a choice anyone had to actively make.

children.text: PMJDY: Turning Bank Accounts Into the Default Way to Receive Money

markDefs.definition: The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, launched 28 August 2014, a national financial inclusion programme offering zero-balance savings accounts, a RuPay debit card, and built-in accident insurance and overdraft facilities.
Direct Benefit Transfer: paying government subsidies, wages, scholarships, and pensions straight into a beneficiary's bank account, rather than through cash or intermediaries.

children.text: opened zero-balance bank accounts at a scale that made global headlines, government data placed the total above 50 crore accounts around the scheme's tenth anniversary in 2024. But opening an account is only step one of the nudge. The real behavioral engine was

: routing LPG subsidies, MGNREGA wages, scholarships, and pensions through these accounts by default, rather than through cash or intermediaries. Nobody had to be convinced a bank account was a good idea in the abstract. Once it became the default channel for money you were already owed, opening one stopped being a discretionary financial decision and became simply the fastest way to get paid.
Aadhaar and the JAM Trinity: The Infrastructure That Made the Default Possible

markDefs.definition: The official shorthand, used in India's Economic Surveys, for the three-pillar infrastructure enabling large-scale Direct Benefit Transfer: Jan Dhan bank accounts, Aadhaar as a single verifiable identity, and near-universal mobile phone access.

children.text: A default at national scale needs infrastructure, not just intent. India's Economic Surveys describe this as the

: Jan Dhan accounts to receive money, Aadhaar as a single, verifiable identity to confirm who should receive it, and near-universal mobile access to confirm delivery and enable authentication. Aadhaar, the 12-digit biometric identity number administered by the UIDAI and placed on a statutory footing by the Aadhaar Act, 2016, is what let one identity layer work across dozens of otherwise disconnected schemes, replacing scheme-by-scheme paperwork with a single, low-friction verification step. This is friction removal from Chapter 1, deployed as core government infrastructure rather than a single app feature.
Was Aadhaar-Linking a Nudge, or Something More?

Run Aadhaar-linked DBT through Chapter 1's own nudge-versus-mandate test, and the answer changes depending on exactly which use of Aadhaar you're looking at. In its 2018 Puttaswamy judgment on the Aadhaar Act, the Supreme Court of India drew precisely this line. It upheld requiring Aadhaar for welfare benefits and subsidies paid from the Consolidated Fund of India under Section 7 of the Aadhaar Act, reasoning that the state has a stronger justification for verifying identity when it is the one disbursing public money. It struck down mandatory Aadhaar linkage for private services, including ordinary bank accounts and mobile SIM connections that were not tied to a government subsidy, ruling that requirement crossed from proportionate verification into an unjustified mandate.

body.text: This is a real-world example of exactly the distinction Chapter 1 drew between a nudge and a mandate, decided by a court rather than a textbook. For a subsidy you are not otherwise owed, requiring Aadhaar is closer to a condition of eligibility than a nudge. For an ordinary bank account you'd open regardless of any government scheme, the same requirement crossed a constitutional line.

children.text: Bundled Defaults Inside the Account Itself

PMJDY doesn't stop at the account. Every account comes with a RuPay debit card carrying built-in accident insurance cover, reportedly up to ₹2 lakh for cards issued after August 2018, and eligible accounts unlock an overdraft facility of up to ₹10,000 after a period of satisfactory operation, both automatic rather than something a holder has to separately apply for. This is the same bundled-default logic as an employer's group insurance in Chapter 2, applied to a state-run account: benefits attach by default, and the holder never has to navigate a separate enrolment process to get them.

body.caption: The JAM Trinity, piece by piece

cells: A default destination account for government money
A single, low-friction identity layer across schemes
A channel for authentication and delivery confirmation

body.title: Nudge or mandate: the ration card case
body.scenario: A state government requires Aadhaar-linked biometric authentication to collect subsidised foodgrain under the public distribution system, with no non-Aadhaar alternative process offered at the local ration shop. A separate, entirely voluntary scheme offers Aadhaar-linked accounts a small annual interest bonus if the holder opts in.
body.prompt: Using the Puttaswamy distinction from this lesson, classify each policy, and explain which one is more exposed to legal or ethical challenge.
body.modelAnswer:
1. The foodgrain case is a subsidy paid from public funds, which the Puttaswamy judgment recognised as a legitimate ground for requiring Aadhaar verification in principle.
2. It becomes exposed to challenge, though, on a separate point the judgment also stressed: authentication failures should not result in denial of a benefit someone is otherwise entitled to, so offering literally no alternative process for someone who cannot authenticate is the vulnerable part, not the Aadhaar requirement itself.
3. The voluntary interest-bonus scheme is a genuine nudge under Chapter 1's own definition: no option is removed, nobody loses access to a benefit they were already entitled to, and Aadhaar-linking is simply one route to an extra incentive among several.
4. The clearest lesson is that "Aadhaar-linked" is not one single category. Whether it functions as a nudge, a justified condition of eligibility, or an overreaching mandate depends entirely on what happens to someone who doesn't or can't comply.

body.title: Default effect or friction removal?
body.question: A state pension scheme automatically deposits monthly payments into a beneficiary's existing Jan Dhan account unless they specifically request a different account. Which mechanism from earlier in this course is most directly at work?
options: The default effect, because the Jan Dhan account is what happens if the beneficiary takes no action
The affect heuristic, because beneficiaries trust the government
The compromise effect, because the Jan Dhan account is a middle option
The certainty effect, because the payment amount is fixed
body.explanation: Automatically using the Jan Dhan account unless the beneficiary actively requests otherwise is a textbook default from Chapter 2: whatever happens without active intervention becomes what almost everyone ends up with.

body.title: Name the infrastructure
body.textWithBlank: The official shorthand for Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar identity, and mobile access working together to enable large-scale Direct Benefit Transfer is the ___ Trinity.
body.explanation: JAM stands for Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile, the three-pillar infrastructure India's Economic Surveys credit with making Direct Benefit Transfer operationally possible at national scale.

body.title: Just how fast did PMJDY open accounts?

children.text: PMJDY reportedly set a Guinness World Record for the most bank accounts opened in a single week, with roughly 1.8 crore accounts opened in the scheme's launch week alone, from 23 to 29 August 2014. That initial burst still needed the JAM Trinity to become a durable behavior change rather than a one-off publicity event. An account opened in week one only stays useful as a default channel once the money that matters to someone, a subsidy, a wage, a pension, is actually routed through it, which is precisely what DBT did over the following years.

body.label: PMJDY's launch date
body.context: The scheme grew to government-reported figures above 50 crore accounts by its tenth anniversary in 2024, making it one of the largest applications of default-based choice architecture anywhere in the world.

cards.definition: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, launched 28 August 2014, offering zero-balance bank accounts with a RuPay card, accident insurance, and an overdraft facility.
Paying subsidies, wages, scholarships, and pensions directly into a beneficiary's bank account by default, rather than through cash or intermediaries.
Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, and Mobile: the three-pillar infrastructure India's Economic Surveys credit with enabling Direct Benefit Transfer at national scale.
India's 12-digit biometric identity number, administered by the UIDAI under the Aadhaar Act, 2016, used as a single verification layer across government schemes.

The Supreme Court ruling upholding mandatory Aadhaar for subsidies paid from the Consolidated Fund of India, while striking down mandatory Aadhaar linkage for private services like ordinary bank accounts.

points: PMJDY's real behavioral power came less from opening accounts and more from making a bank account the default channel through which government money reached people, via Direct Benefit Transfer.
The JAM Trinity, Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, and Mobile, is the infrastructure stack that made a single, low-friction default possible across dozens of otherwise disconnected government schemes.

Not all Aadhaar-linking is the same kind of policy. The 2018 Puttaswamy judgment upheld it as a condition for subsidies from public funds, while striking it down as a mandate for private services, a real-world application of Chapter 1's nudge-versus-mandate distinction.
PMJDY accounts bundle accident insurance and overdraft facilities as automatic defaults, the same logic as employer group insurance in Chapter 2, run through a state-managed account instead.

The next lessons in this chapter look at two more Indian nudges built on this same infrastructure: how UPI removed friction from digital payments, and how Swachh Bharat used social norms rather than defaults to change behavior at scale.
